name: Ivan Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 43, a senior developer at a tech company that writes appliance-warranty claims software. I have a master's degree and lead releases; yesterday a pair of photos of one cracked kettle almost became two claims. I use AI every day to sketch test cases, then check the claim rules myself. My partner runs the school library; our two children are in school, and we have a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team an AI draft can save us time on a warranty claim, but the serial number and sale date still have to match. I use it every day to propose test cases, then check those against real claim rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current pay and household bills would stay much as they are. I'm well paid, my partner runs the school library, and we have ten months of expenses set aside; the mortgage is covered while both jobs hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the claim-release checks and use AI to propose tests, as I already do. We'd put another 200 a month into the reserve while both wages hold, then review the budget after the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, provided a customer can still appeal a refused claim. A faster answer is only useful when the receipt and serial number agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your test catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer sent two photos of the same cracked kettle from different angles. The draft system counted them as two damaged items, and my test caught that before the claim was refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you keep the reserve separate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I keep the reserve in a separate account from holiday money. We want the mortgage paid even if one of us needs time to find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that AI could handle ordinary claim code and leave a smaller team for unusual faults. I want the appeal route tested before anyone boasts about a cheaper claims desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior title may not protect my pay if much of the code is generated. There are other software firms nearby and we have savings, yet many employers could trim the same posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the team log overturned refusals and compare them with AI drafts in our next scheduled release review. If the appeal errors fall and our manager approves, I'd put the tool into one claim queue with a named human reviewer; we'd hold off replacing our family car until we see the staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about cuts, although I can test this without staking our mortgage on a guess. I don't want the children to see a car purchase become a bill we cannot carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as an overturned refusal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count an appeal as overturned only when the customer supplies a receipt or serial number that changes the decision. A friendly sounding reply is not proof the claim was handled well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why can the car wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our old car still gets the children to school and my partner to the library. We can defer the replacement for a year without disrupting either job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 may write claims code before repair robots arrive around 2031. I'd rather know which real problems still pay a person than call every new tool a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my software post could go quickly, even though I lead releases. Ten months saved gives us a search period, but my partner's library wage alone will not cover mortgage and both children's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd list the local firms that still advertise paid claims or payment-system roles and check the actual salary ranges. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for signed jobs with household pay covering mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd take other paid local work while using the reserve and speak to the lender before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage. I have a cushion, but the deadline arrives before we can turn a side idea into dependable rent or mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your brother’s workshop replace your salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother repairs appliances for a living and has offered to show me the workshop, but A visit to my brother's appliance workshop is not a second income. He has orders because he can diagnose a fault and fix it, not because I can write a booking page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trigger a family move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children that school stays put while we look at actual offers. We would discuss a move only if a signed job elsewhere paid enough after moving costs, not because someone mentioned a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 gives us a chance to test a real repair-booking service, while thinking AI can still displace my code before robots reach workshops around 2034. I won't tell friends an app is a business until someone pays for a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have time to build another source of earnings with my brother, but he's the skilled repairer and has his own work to protect. I cannot gamble the mortgage reserve or assume his workshop can carry my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my brother whether he wants a limited booking service and confirm what permissions and payment records we'd need. If he agrees, the permissions are in place and actual paid repair orders appear, I'd spend no more than five percent of our savings on a separate booking line while keeping at least nine months of expenses untouched; after 2031 I'd continue it only while orders pay their costs, and keep my software job or seek a signed local post covering family bills if that job ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years is enough to find out if the small service has customers. I would rather have a receipt for a repair than a slide deck about one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would set the repair price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother would set the repair price and decide which jobs he can safely take. I could handle bookings and receipts, but I would not advertise service he cannot deliver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What limit would your partner want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants a cap on the money before we try anything. We agree that the mortgage reserve cannot become an experiment account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 lets us see which appliance repairs people actually request, even if thinking AI makes ordinary code cheap. Robots able to do hands-on work follow around 2039, so I would not count on physical repair being immune forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53, my software salary might be gone, but I am secure on today's income and ten-month reserve. Any extra booking money is a possibility, not something already in the family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue release checks and set aside 200 monthly while both wages hold. If my brother agrees, legal permissions are clear and paid repair bookings cover their own costs for six months, I'd keep the booking service with the same five-percent capital cap and nine-month reserve; in the first year after 2036, I'd keep software work if it still pays, and close bookings if orders stop covering costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about what we can pay today. A long runway lets me insist on real transactions before putting family savings into a service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your child about repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child likes taking apart a broken toaster. I tell them to learn why it failed and how to work safely, not to assume my booking code repairs the heating element.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you extend the booking line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my partner six months of paid orders and the remaining reserve before extending the service. If the numbers do not work, I can shut the booking line without touching mortgage money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because claims code could lose its value before another employer offers a paid post. Real salary ranges, notice before cuts and a lender conversation before arrears would help us protect the children's routine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether my brother wants more orders. My brother’s workshop is his livelihood, not a prop for my software plan; I would ask him first and keep our mortgage reserve separate.

headlineQuote: My brother’s workshop is his livelihood, not a prop for my software plan; I would ask him first and keep our mortgage reserve separate.
portrait: Ivan, **43**, leads software releases for appliance-warranty claims after a master's degree and checks AI-generated tests daily.
His **higher pay**, partner's school-library wage, ten-month reserve and nearby firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He counts **appeal reversals** before letting AI into one claim queue, and fast 2028 AGI alarms him because his wage is larger.
His brother repairs appliances, but Ivan considers **booking income** only with consent, permissions, paid orders and a protected reserve.
A decade leaves him **calm about current bills** while he tests demand and keeps paid software work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his larger software wage before a signed replacement job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Real salary ranges**, notice before cuts and lender access before arrears would protect the family routine.
